name: Southern US English
summary: Southern US English is a family of accents and dialects. Sound is where it differs most: the PRICE vowel loses its glide (stage 1 of the Southern Vowel Shift, complete in most Southern dialects), the FACE/DRESS and KIT/FLEECE vowels move in later stages, short front vowels can 'break' into two parts (the drawl), pin and pen merge before nasals, and cot and caught stay distinct. Grammar is where an actor can add real flavour with few words: fixin' to, y'all, double modals (might could), liketa, perfective done, personal datives (I love me some...), and, in Appalachian/Ozark speech, a-prefixing. Round 2 added the Yale Grammatical Diversity Project (YGDP) pages for each grammar item and a Wikipedia page on the Southern Vowel Shift that summarises Labov, Ash and Boberg (2006) and Thomas (2004). Those two primary works were NOT opened directly. Many features are declining among younger and urban speakers; 'Southern' is not one accent (see sub_regions).

grammar.condition: Only for two or more people. Possessive is y'all's. Widespread and not heavily stigmatized (source 1).
grammar.example_standard: Are you coming to dinner tonight?
grammar.example_dialect: Are y'all coming to dinner tonight?

grammar.condition: Used when addressing several distinct groups. Rare; once at most per monologue.

grammar.standard: be about to / be going to (near future)
grammar.dialect: fixin' to (also finna in African American English)
grammar.condition: YGDP: near future, most common in the present tense; can take non-human subjects ('It's fixin' to rain'). Speaker needs good grounds, so 'maybe' sounds odd. NEGATIVE 'not fixin' to' carries a strong 'I'm never going to' refusal. Not possible in the future tense (*will be fixin' to).
grammar.example_standard: I'm about to wash the dishes.
grammar.example_dialect: I'm fixin' to wash the dishes.

grammar.dialect: might could (also might can, might should, might would, may could)
grammar.condition: YGDP: double modals are widespread in the South, usually start with might or may, are not stigmatized, but frequency varies a lot by speaker. Attested in Texas, the Carolinas, Alabama, Tennessee.
grammar.example_standard: I thought you might be able to help me.
grammar.example_dialect: I thought you might could help me.

grammar.condition: YGDP: only in affirmative or negative statements, not questions; comes before a past-event verb and not before 'be'. Often dramatic or dangerous situations. Appalachian, white Southern and African American English.

grammar.standard: have already (emphatic, often surprised or irritated)
grammar.condition: YGDP: found in African American English and in some white Southern speech (e.g. Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina). Usually with past-form action verbs; adds emotion or surprise. Many speakers avoid it in negatives. Not used by every Southern speaker.

grammar.standard: reflexive pronoun after a verb (for oneself)
grammar.dialect: personal dative: 'I love me some...', 'caught her a catfish'
grammar.condition: YGDP: pronoun right after the verb that refers back to the subject, usually with 'some' or 'a', for events the subject benefits from. Commoner in the South and Appalachia but YGDP says the regional pattern is weaker than for other Southern datives.
grammar.example_dialect: I love me some baked beans.

grammar.condition: YGDP: Appalachian, Ozark and Smoky Mountain speech; only on -ing VERBS (not nouns/adjectives), usually on verbs stressed on the first syllable. Old-fashioned and rural: do NOT use as a general 'Southern' marker.

Negative concord (double negation). YGDP lists Alabama White English, African American, Appalachian, West Texas. Stigmatized in formal settings; marks informal or rural-working-class characters. Not specific to the South.
Source 1 lists 'It's one lady who lives in town' as a Southern pattern. One-sentence source; medium-low confidence.
grammar.example_standard: There's a lady who lives in town.
grammar.example_dialect: It's one lady who lives in town.

grammar.standard: am not / is not / are not / have not
grammar.condition: Widespread non-standard, not South-specific; source 1 lists it as typical Southern vocabulary. Use sparingly.
Source 1 gives 'yesterday they riz up, come outside, drawed, and drownded' and says 'drug' is traditionally both past tense and participle of drag. Rural, older flavour; keep to one at most.
grammar.example_standard: Yesterday they rose up and drowned.
grammar.example_dialect: Yesterday they riz up and drownded.

vocabulary.standard: turn on / off / out (a light or device)
vocabulary.dialect: cut on / cut off / cut out
vocabulary.note: Source 1: 'cut on/off/out' for lights and electronics.
Source 1: 'ordinary' can mean disreputable. Easy to misread; use with context.

Source 1: sympathy, 'now often used sarcastically'. Meaning depends on tone.

pronunciation.rule: PRICE monophthong (Southern Shift stage 1): the glide of /aɪ/ weakens or disappears, so 'ride' can sound like 'rod' or 'rad' to other Americans. Inland Southern speakers (Appalachia, central Texas) may drop the glide in ALL positions; in coastal cities such as Charleston, Atlanta and Savannah it is absent or rare. Stage 1 is complete in most Southern dialects.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Hold one open 'ah' for 'my', 'ride', 'time', 'I'. Do not glide to 'ee'. Not every Southern character does it: for Atlanta/Charleston-type urban speakers use a normal glide.
pronunciation.example: my, ride, time, I, nice white rice

pronunciation.rule: Southern Shift stage 2: FACE drops to [ɛɪ]; DRESS rises and breaks ('pet' close to 'pay-et'). Mainly on stressed syllables.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Make 'day' start lower ('deh-ee'). For 'pet', 'bed' add a small 'uh' after the vowel. Use only on stressed words.

pronunciation.rule: Southern Shift stage 3 (common inland): KIT becomes a rising diphthong [iə]; FLEECE starts lower [ɪi].
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'Pit' sounds like 'pee-it'; 'see' starts with a short 'ih'. Subtle: one word per line is enough.

pronunciation.rule: Southern drawl: stressed short front vowels (TRAP, DRESS, KIT) become two-part vowels, so one syllable can sound like two. Most prominent in speakers born before 1960 and declining (Thomas 2004 via source 11).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Stretch ONE stressed word, e.g. 'pet' -> 'pay-et', 'pit' -> 'pee-it'. A drawl on every word is a caricature.

pronunciation.rule: Pin-pen merger: /ɛ/ and /ɪ/ merge before nasals (m, n, ng); the merged vowel is mostly [ɪ]. Absent or incomplete in New Orleans, South Florida and the South Carolina/Georgia Lowcountry (Wikipedia summary of Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Say 'pen' and 'pin' identically (closer to 'pin'). Only before m, n, ng: 'bet' and 'bit' stay different.

pronunciation.rule: Mary-merry merger (partial): Mary and merry share a vowel; 'marry' may keep its own. Most common in the South, especially Louisiana.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Subtle; use only if the text has these words.

pronunciation.rule: Back vowels are fronted: GOAT, GOOSE, STRUT and FOOT sit further forward than in many other American accents.
pronunciation.ipa: GOAT, GOOSE, STRUT, FOOT fronted (direction only)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep the vowel but move it forward ('go', 'you', 'cup').

pronunciation.rule: No cot-caught merger: Southern English (like Midland) resists the merger, so 'cot' and 'caught' stay different.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep 'cot' short and unrounded and 'caught' rounder; do not use a Californian merged vowel.

pronunciation.rule: R: most Southern accents are rhotic today. Older speakers and some African American Southern speakers may be largely non-rhotic. White Southern speech, traditionally non-rhotic, has become 'intensely rhotic'.
pronunciation.ipa: /r/ pronounced (default); older/rural/AAE: coda r weak or absent
pronunciation.actor_tip: Default: keep every r. Only for an older rural or Black Southern character should coda r fade ('cah', 'doh').

pronunciation.rule: Front stress: first-syllable stress in words such as 'hotel' and 'guitar' (shared with African American English).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Push the weight onto the first syllable; it is rhythm, not a vowel change.

intonation.rule: Front stress on some multi-syllable words ('HO-tel', 'GUI-tar') gives Southern speech a different rhythm from General American (source 1, shared with AAE).
intonation.actor_tip: Shift the stress to syllable 1 for those words only.

intonation.rule: The drawl lengthens and 'breaks' stressed short vowels, especially in emphasised words; weaker or absent in younger urban speakers. Use it as emphasis on a key word, not as a constant slow tempo.
intonation.actor_tip: One drawled word per line at most.

common_mistakes: Stretching every vowel in the line (the 'Foghorn' caricature). The drawl is for one stressed word.
Using y'all to address one person.
Using a-prefixing ('a-goin'') as a general Southern marker. YGDP ties it to Appalachian/Ozark/Smoky Mountain speech.
Dropping every r for every character. Most Southern accents are rhotic today.
Using 'not fixin' to' as a polite 'not yet'. It means a firm refusal.
Spelling words in eye-dialect ('gonna', 'yer', 'ah'). Keep standard spelling; carry the accent in delivery notes.
Applying the PRICE monophthong to every Southern character. Atlanta/Charleston-type urban speech does not drop the glide.
Piling on ain't, fixin' to, y'all and bless your heart in one speech. Choose one or two.
generational_notes: Source 1: the Southern accent is receding, especially among younger and more urban Southerners.
Drawl: strongest in speakers born before 1960 and declining (source 11 citing Thomas 2004).
R-dropping: older white Southern speech was non-rhotic; younger white speakers are strongly rhotic (source 1).
A-prefixing in Ozark English was absent in speakers under 15, but used by all ages in the Appalachian data (YGDP, source 9).
Perfective done and 'riz/drownded' type forms read as older, rural or working-class; 'y'all' and 'fixin' to' are the most age-stable.
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first; add Southern flavour with 1-3 items per monologue, not everything at once.
Decide the character: older/rural, middle-aged, or young/urban. Only older/rural characters get r-fading, drawl, a-prefixing or 'riz/drownded'.
Best-value grammar: y'all (group), fixin' to (near future; 'not fixin' to' = refusal), might could (hedge), 'I love me some X' (enthusiasm), liketa/done (drama).
Vocabulary: 2-3 words at most (reckon, buggy, ornery, 'Coke' for any soda); pick words that fit the scene.
No eye-dialect respelling. Do not write 'ah', 'yer', 'gonna'. Put sound instructions in actor notes: PRICE as one open 'ah', pin=pen before m/n/ng, one drawled word.
Apply pin-pen only before m, n, ng. Apply PRICE monophthong only to inland/rural/older characters (and with a normal glide for city characters).
In actor notes, list which rules were applied so they can be practised one by one.

open_questions: Primary sources (Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006; Thomas 2004; Dictionary of American Regional English) were not opened. Vowel IPA comes via a Wikipedia summary; check the ANAE Southern chapter or native recordings before relying on exact values.

Whether PRICE monophthongisation differs before voiced vs voiceless consonants: the opened pages say only 'many or all environments' (inland: all positions). The widely repeated claim that it is most common before voiced consonants was not verified.
No verified intonation/pitch description for Southern speech beyond front stress and drawl. Check IDEA or Thomas 2004 recordings.
Differences between Deep South and Texas were not systematically verified (only Texas data in the multiple-modals page and 'tump').
Age distribution of vocabulary (yonder, varmint, taters, reckon, tote) is not in the sources. Labels here are coaching judgement.
'Bless your heart' meaning shift (sincere vs sarcastic) is stated in source 1; frequency by region/age is not.
Existential 'it' and 'riz/drownded' rest on a single Wikipedia sentence each.
Pin-pen areas: a Penn phonological atlas map page was not accessible (403); the merger area for Texas and South Midland comes only from a search-result excerpt, not an opened page.

examples.korean_idea: 너희 오늘 저녁 먹으러 올 거야? (여러 명에게)

examples.regional_english: Are y'all coming to dinner tonight?
examples.note: 'y'all'은 두 명 이상에게만 씁니다(출처 1). 한 사람에게 쓰면 틀립니다.

examples.korean_idea: 난 그거 안 할 거야! (강한 거절)
examples.neutral_english: I'm not going to do that!
examples.regional_english: I'm not fixin' to do that!
examples.note: YGDP: 'not fixin' to'는 '절대 ~하지 않겠다'는 강한 거절 뉘앙스입니다.
liketa는 '하마터면'. 의문문이나 be동사 앞에는 못 씁니다(YGDP).
perfective done은 놀람/짜증 감정이 실립니다. AAE와 일부 백인 남부 화자(YGDP).
진심 동정에도, 빈정거림에도 쓰입니다. 톤으로 구분(출처 1). 한 번만 쓰세요.

examples.neutral_english: You're in a bad mood today.
examples.note: ornery = bad-tempered. 가벼운 농담조의 시비에 좋습니다(출처 1).
YGDP 예문과 같은 구조(사물 주어도 가능).

examples.korean_idea: 내가 좀 도와줄 수 있을지도 몰라.
examples.neutral_english: I might be able to help you with that.
examples.regional_english: I might could help you with that.
examples.note: 이중 조동사. 남부에서 흔하고 낙인이 약하지만 사람마다 빈도 차이가 큽니다(YGDP).

examples.regional_english: I love me some baked beans.
examples.note: personal dative. YGDP 예문 그대로의 구조입니다.

examples.neutral_english: I'm going to get a soda.
examples.regional_english: I'm gonna get me a Coke.
examples.note: Coke는 탄산음료 전반을 뜻할 수 있음(출처 1) + personal dative(YGDP).
부정 일치. YGDP의 Alabama White English 예문과 같은 구조.

sub_regions.name: 내륙 남부 vs 해안 도시
sub_regions.note: PRICE 활음 탈락은 내륙(애팔래치아, 중부 텍사스)에서 모든 위치에 나타나고 찰스턴·애틀랜타·서배너 같은 동부 해안 도시에서는 거의 없습니다.

sub_regions.name: pin-pen 예외 지역
sub_regions.note: 뉴올리언스, 남부 플로리다, 사우스캐롤라이나·조지아 로컬랜드는 병합이 거의 없거나 불완전합니다.

sub_regions.note: po' boy, banquette, neutral ground 같은 지역 어휘. Mary-merry 병합이 특히 흔합니다.

sub_regions.name: 애팔래치아·오자크·스모키마운틴
sub_regions.note: a-prefixing, liketa, personal dative 등 가장 '시골/산악' 색이 강한 문법. 일반 남부 인물에게는 쓰지 마세요.

sub_regions.name: 텍사스와 남서부
sub_regions.note: 이중 조동사(Di Paolo 1989 텍사스 자료)와 tump가 확인됨. 딥사우스와의 체계적 차이는 이번에 검증하지 못했습니다(open_questions).

sub_regions.name: 백인 vs 흑인 남부 화자
sub_regions.note: perfective done과 finna는 AAE에서 중심. 전통적 r 탈락은 일부 흑인 남부 화자에게 남아 있고 백인 남부 화자는 r을 강하게 발음하는 쪽으로 변했습니다.

confidence_detail: medium-high for grammar (each item checked on a Yale Grammatical Diversity Project page); medium for pronunciation (Wikipedia summaries of ANAE/Thomas; primary works not opened); medium-low for vocabulary age/region labels (Wikipedia list, no age data).
